issues.issue: The preamble contains an OCR/typographical error in the enabling statute citation ("Chapter 40]" for Chapter 40J), but it does not change the identity of either party. Nothing in the identification of the parties is genuinely susceptible of two readings.

The recital defines the "Network Operator Agreement" as a Master Agreement the parties "are considering entering into," i.e. a document not yet executed and whose terms are not fixed. That sits awkwardly with the operative guaranty in section 2.1, which guarantees obligations "under the Network Operator Agreement" as if it already existed and as it "may be changed."

The recital describes the guaranteed contract only in general terms ("certain network operator services" and "certain financial, operational and other responsibilities"), leaving the scope of what is guaranteed to be supplied from an extrinsic document. The catch-all "and other responsibilities" has no fixed boundary.

The recital says the guarantee is issued "in order to enhance the security sought by MTC," a purpose statement that could be used to argue for a broader reading than the capped, conditional obligation in section 2.1. The tension is faint and the recital defers expressly to "as provided herein."

The guaranty covers both payment and "performance" obligations and extends to "any and all costs, expenses and liabilities ... including, but not limited to, the costs of causing the substituted performance"; the reach of that open-ended catch-all is not fixed. A court could be asked whether it captures consequential losses or only substitution costs.

A guaranty of non-monetary "performance" obligations is hard to square with the purely monetary cap and discharge mechanism in the following sentences of section 2.1 (the $4,000,000 cap and the "advance to MTC funds" release). How performance obligations are measured against a dollar cap is left unresolved.

The cap is stated flatly but it is not said whether it applies only to the "Guaranteed Obligations" of clause (a) or also to the costs, expenses and liabilities of clause (b), nor whether interest and enforcement costs count against it. "This guaranty is limited to and capped at" leaves that allocation genuinely open.

The cap must be reconciled with section 2.2's "continuing, absolute and unconditional" guaranty that remains in force "until all obligations of Network Operator ... have been fulfilled," which the parenthetical only loosely qualifies. Whether the cap or the continuing-obligation language controls is not spelled out.

"[S]hould Guarantor advance to MTC funds up to said amount" is ambiguous as to whether any payment short of $4,000,000 (an amount "up to" the cap) discharges the Guarantor, or only payment of the full capped sum. The release turns entirely on that phrase.

The discharge on payment conflicts with section 2.2, which makes the guaranty continue "until all obligations of Network Operator under the Network Operator Agreement have been fulfilled"; the parenthetical cross-reference to section 2.1 is the only bridge. A court could be asked which of the two endpoints governs.

The parenthetical "(except as noted in section 2.1 above)" does not identify which part of section 2.1 qualifies the "absolute and unconditional" character of the guaranty — the cap, the discharge on payment, or the default condition. The exception's scope must be construed.

The clause keeps the guaranty in force "until all obligations of Network Operator ... have been fulfilled" while section 2.1 releases the Guarantor once it advances funds up to $4,000,000. Those two termination points cannot both be literally true.

The introductory list of preserved-liability events is preceded by "Without limiting the scope of this Agreement as set forth above," and the enumerated items A–C are specific waivers, extensions and modifications; whether the list is exhaustive or illustrative is not stated. The stray capital "The" mid-sentence is a mechanical slip that does not change meaning.

Item A preserves liability despite MTC's waiver of performance "by Network Operator, Guarantor," which sits oddly with section 4.4's requirement that any waiver in favour of Guarantor be in a writing signed by MTC. The tension is slight and readily harmonised.

"[A]s defined below" points forward to section 3.2 rather than naming it, and the right to "proceed directly" against the Guarantor is stated without saying whether demand or exhaustion against Network Operator is required. Both points are readily resolved from the surrounding text.

The right to proceed directly on an Event of Default must be read with the Guarantor's cure right in the very next sentence and with section 3.2.A's cure period; whether MTC may sue while the Guarantor's cure window runs is not addressed. The clauses are sequential and largely harmonisable.

The cure right is measured by "the time period, if any, provided Network Operator in the Network Operator Agreement," and the phrase "if any" leaves the Guarantor with no cure window at all where the other agreement specifies none. Whether the section 3.2.A thirty-day fallback supplies one is unstated.

The clause opens "Notwithstanding any other provision of this Guaranty or the Network Operator Agreement," which purports to override terms of a separate contract that this Guaranty does not amend. Its interaction with the incorporation by reference in section 4.6 is unaddressed.

The waiver enumerates presentment, demand, dishonor and protest and then adds "all other notices in connection with the delivery, acceptance, performance, or default," a catch-all whose reach against the specifics is uncertain. Whether it sweeps in notices the Guarantor is separately promised is the question.

The blanket waiver of "all other notices ... in connection with ... default" contradicts the very next sentence of section 2.6, which entitles Guarantor to contemporaneous notice of any default declared by MTC. The two sentences pull in opposite directions.

The entitlement to contemporaneous default notice sits against the immediately preceding waiver in section 2.6 of "all other notices in connection with ... default," and against section 3.2.A which measures cure from notice to Network Operator, not to Guarantor. The final clause of 2.6 partly, but not wholly, reconciles them.
"[S]hall only postpone the time for performance" does not say by how long performance is postponed or from what event the new time runs. The mechanism of the postponement is left undefined.
"[A]s often as may be deemed expedient" does not say by whom expediency is judged or by what standard. The phrase is vague but it merely preserves rights rather than creating an obligation.

The clause speaks of a breach "by any party" waived "by the other party so empowered to act," although this Guaranty imposes obligations only on the Guarantor and section 4.4 requires waivers to be signed by MTC. The reciprocal phrasing is loose rather than genuinely ambiguous.

The thirty-day fallback cure period in A runs from notice "to Network Operator," while section 2.5 gives Guarantor a cure right measured by the Network Operator Agreement and section 2.6 promises Guarantor contemporaneous notice. Whether Guarantor gets the same thirty days is not stated.

The clause makes the Agreement binding upon and inuring to the benefit of "Network Operator," which is not a signatory to this Guaranty (see the preamble, which names only Guarantor and MTC as parties). Whether Network Operator has rights or duties under the Guaranty is left unclear.
Section 4.6 separately restates severability ("in such cases the principle of Severability shall govern"), duplicating this section. The duplication is redundant rather than contradictory.

Amendments and waivers are effective only if "in writing and signed by MTC," omitting any signature by the Guarantor even for amendments that would enlarge its obligations. Whether a one-signature amendment can bind the Guarantor is a question the wording invites.

Notices must be "sent via overnight courier or personally delivered," an exclusive two-method list that excludes mail, fax and email; whether a notice given another way is ineffective is left to inference. The listing invites an expressio unius argument.

"[E]ffective the business day following the date sent delivered via overnight courier" is garbled — "sent delivered" leaves it unclear whether effectiveness runs from dispatch or from delivery. The one-day rule turns on which event starts it.

The clause refers to the laws of the "State of Massachusetts," which is styled a Commonwealth in the preamble; the slip is immaterial to meaning. "[G]overned by, construed in and enforced in accordance exclusively with" is otherwise a standard, definite choice of law.

Arbitration is conditioned on the parties failing "to resolve any dispute between them through mediation" or being "unable to convene mediation within 60 days of first attempting to do so," yet nothing in this Guaranty provides for mediation, identifies who must initiate it, or defines what counts as "first attempting" it. Whether the condition precedent was satisfied turns wholly on those undefined phrases.

The clause makes arbitration available only "at MTC's sole election" and permits consolidation with the MTC/Network Operator arbitration, which is difficult to reconcile with the next sentence's default that "all disputes shall be resolved by litigation" and with the wholesale incorporation of the Network Operator Agreement's dispute resolution provisions in the last sentence of section 4.6. Which regime governs a given dispute must be construed.

The litigation default is expressly subordinated to MTC's arbitration election in the preceding sentence, but the last sentence of section 4.6 incorporates "all other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration" from the Network Operator Agreement, which may itself mandate arbitration. The two cannot be applied together without deciding which controls.

"Except to the extent MTC elects arbitration ... for a given dispute" gives no timing or manner for the election, so the forum for any dispute remains indeterminate until MTC acts. The phrase "a given dispute" also leaves open whether a single controversy can be split between forums.

"All other provisions relating to dispute resolution or arbitration" in a separate agreement are incorporated without identifying them, so the reach of "relating to" and the meaning of "other" (other than what?) are open. A court must decide which terms of the Network Operator Agreement came across.

The incorporated provisions may conflict with the express terms of section 4.6 itself — MTC's sole election to arbitrate, the Boston AAA venue, the expedited Commercial Rules, and the Middlesex County litigation default — and the clause gives no order of precedence. That is a direct conflict within the same section.
